No — both fail under the GDPR.

- Recital 32 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 requires consent to be given by a clear affirmative act establishing a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of agreement, such as ticking a box or choosing technical settings.
- Recital 32 (continued, in passage [1]) expressly states that silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not constitute consent — so the pre-ticked marketing-profiling box is not valid consent.
- Article 7(3) gives the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time, and it must be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.
- Since consent could be given by simply ticking a box online, requiring withdrawal only by posting a signed letter makes withdrawal harder than giving consent, contrary to Article 7(3).
- Article 7(3) also provides that withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal, and the data subject must be informed of the right to withdraw beforehand.

Yes — the retail use is caught by the prohibition; the research-only use is not.

- Article 5(1)(f) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service for that purpose, or using AI systems that infer emotions of natural persons in the workplace and education institutions (evidence [1], [4]).
- The only exception is where the AI system is intended to be put in place or on the market for medical or safety reasons (evidence [1], [4]); the recitals confirm the prohibition does not cover systems placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, such as therapeutic use (evidence [5]).
- Monitoring shop staff mood is a workplace use and is not for medical or safety reasons, so the retailer's use falls squarely within the prohibition (evidence [1], [5]).
- The recitals explain the rationale: the imbalance of power at work combined with the intrusive nature of such systems could lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment of persons or whole groups (evidence [5]).
- However, the Regulation excludes from its scope AI systems specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development (evidence [7]).
- Therefore the university lab's research-only use is outside the Regulation's scope, while the retailer's later workplace use is prohibited under Article 5(1)(f).

The platform must give the user access to its internal complaint-handling system to challenge the removal decision, available for at least six months, starting from the day the user is informed of the decision, and free of charge.

- Article 20(1) requires providers of online platforms to give recipients of the service access to an internal complaint-handling system to lodge complaints against decisions on the grounds that information constitutes illegal content, including decisions whether or not to remove or disable access to or restrict visibility of the information.
- Article 20(1) states the system must be available for a period of at least six months following the decision.
- Article 20(2) provides that the six-month period starts on the day the recipient of the service is informed about the decision in accordance with Article 16(5) or Article 17.
- Article 20(1) requires complaints to be lodged electronically and free of charge.
- Article 20(3) adds that the system must be easy to access, user-friendly, and enable sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated complaints.

The company had to notify the Commission without delay and in any event within 2 months after the thresholds were met (Article 3(3), Digital Markets Act). If it fails to notify and fails to provide the information requested under Article 21 within the Commission's deadline, the Commission may still designate it as a gatekeeper based on available information (Article 3). The maximum fine for failing to notify is not stated in the provided evidence — NOT_FOUND.

No, the short-term right to reject is no longer available.

- Under section 22(1) and (3), the short-term right to reject is lost if not exercised within 30 days beginning with the first day after ownership/possession has been transferred and the goods have been delivered (and any required installation action notified). Ten weeks exceeds this, so the right is lost (unless the trader agreed it could be exercised later).
- The next tier of remedies under section 19(3) is the right to repair or replacement (section 23), followed by the right to a price reduction or the final right to reject (sections 20 and 24).
- Under section 23(6)–(7), the consumer must give the trader a reasonable time to repair or replace, unless doing so would cause significant inconvenience.
- If repair or replacement is unsuccessful, section 24(5)–(6) allows a price reduction or final right to reject, and under section 24(8) any refund on a final rejection may be reduced for the use the consumer has had of the goods.

The evidence provided does not address whether the consumer must prove the fault existed at delivery, so that point cannot be answered from the passages given.

Digital Services Act - threshold: average monthly active recipients of the service in the Union equal to or higher than 45 million (equivalent to 10 % of the Union population, calculated as an average over a period of six months), designating very large online platforms or very large online search engines.
Digital Markets Act - threshold: 45 million is not a user-count threshold; the DMA counts 'active end users' and 'active business users' per core platform service, expressed as a percentage of the entire population of the Union (end users) and of the entire population of businesses using core platform services (business users).
Digital Markets Act - additional requirements alongside the user figure: a market capitalisation or its equivalent fair market value of at least EUR 75 billion in the last financial year, and provision of the same core platform service in at least three Member States.

The DSA's 45 million is a direct user threshold for designating very large online platforms/search engines, whereas the DMA's user figures are percentages of the Union population, and the DMA additionally requires a EUR 75 billion market capitalisation and presence in at least three Member States.

AI Act prohibited AI practice: 7 %
Digital Services Act (Commission, very large online platform): 6 %
Digital Markets Act (gatekeeper, first offence): 10 %

The maximum fine share is highest under the Digital Markets Act (10 %), followed by the AI Act (7 %) and then the Digital Services Act (6 %).

The AI Act (Article 3) defines 'special categories of personal data' by cross-reference rather than writing its own definition: it means the categories of personal data referred to in Article 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 and Article 10(1) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725. In other words, it points to the definitions already established in the GDPR, the Law Enforcement Directive, and the EUDR.

AI Act (general case) - Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Art. 73(2): not later than 15 days after becoming aware of the serious incident
GDPR - Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Art. 33(1): where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of the breach

The GDPR deadline (72 hours) is shorter than the AI Act general deadline (15 days) — by 13 days and 12 hours.
